before.exam_tip_html: For Paper 3 inference questions on this period, focus on what a source implies about the strain on the regime — not what it states. Quote one short detail (a bread ration figure, a casualty number, a line about Rasputin) and draw one inference from it; a paragraph of paraphrase will score lower than a tight, supported point. For 12-mark causation essays on why the Tsar fell, weigh war, economic crisis and the Rasputin scandal against each other rather than describing each in turn — examiners reward a substantiated judgement on the most important cause, not a list.

For Paper 3 inference questions on the Provisional Government, look for sources that hint at its lack of mandate or its dependence on the Soviet — Order Number 1, the Milyukov Note leak, soldier committees ignoring orders. For 12-mark causation essays on its failure, weigh the war (June Offensive), the postponed Constituent Assembly, the land question and the Kornilov Affair against each other rather than describing each in turn. Examiners reward students who reach a substantiated judgement on the most important cause and use period vocabulary — Dual Power, Order Number 1, Constituent Assembly, Kadet, Soviet — throughout to lift their SPaG and depth marks together.

For Paper 3 inference questions on collectivisation, look for sources that hint at the gap between regime claims and rural reality — the slaughtered livestock, the closed villages, the seized seed grain. One sharp inference about that gap will outscore a paragraph of paraphrase. For 12-mark causation essays on why Stalin abandoned the NEP, weigh the 1927–28 grain procurement crisis, the political logic of breaking the peasantry, the demand for grain exports to fund industry, and the ideological commitment to socialism in the countryside — reach a substantiated judgement, do not list. For 16- and 20-mark interpretation questions, examine BOTH interpretations as views, not as evidence to be cross-examined for bias. Avoid slipping into moral commentary (‘Stalin was evil’); examiners reward analysis of cause, consequence and significance. Use period vocabulary — kolkhoz, sovkhoz, Sovnarkom, dekulakisation, Holodomor — to lift SPaG and depth marks together.
